summary.en: Use recursive reductions for arithmetic, text reversal, Hanoi, search and patterns.
summary.bn: ঘাত, অঙ্কের যোগ, GCD, লেখা উল্টানো, Hanoi ও সার্চ রিকারশন দিয়ে করো।

notes: All reductions work in C17; recursion depth and available execution storage remain implementation limits.

sections.title: Choose a reduction that matches the problem
Trace digit sum and Euclid GCD
Understand the Tower of Hanoi plan
Binary search must shrink past its midpoint
Preserve the problem's meaning in every call
One stopping rule for each reduction

examples.title: Integer powers with a zero exponent
examples.explanationHtml: The results are 81 and 1. The exponent decreases to zero, whose empty product is defined as one here.

examples.title: Peel digits and reduce a GCD pair
examples.explanationHtml: The digit sum is 14. GCD reduces (84,30) to (30,24), (24,6) and (6,0), giving 6.

examples.title: Reverse a small writable string
examples.explanationHtml: text is a writable character array with a trailing zero character. Swapping pairs preserves that terminator and prints akahD.

examples.title: Move three disks between pegs
examples.explanationHtml: Seven moves obey the smaller-on-larger rule. The second recursive call uses the spare peg as its new source.

examples.title: Search a sorted array recursively
examples.explanationHtml: The found index is 3 and the missing result is -1. Each call excludes the midpoint that was already checked.

examples.title: Build a triangle while calls return
examples.explanationHtml: The first visible row has one star because triangle handles smaller rows before printing the current row.

practice.title: A bounded recursive power
practice.statementHtml: Read base from -10 to 10 and exponent from 0 to 10. Treat every exponent-zero result as 1, including base zero. Print Base and exponent: then the signed integer power.
hints: These bounds keep even 10 to the tenth within long long.

practice.title: Digits and greatest common divisor
practice.statementHtml: Read two unsigned integers from 0 to 1000000. Print Numbers: first, then the digit sum of the first and GCD of the pair. Define GCD(0,0) as zero for this task.
hints: A nonzero second argument becomes the next first argument.

practice.title: Recursively reverse one word
practice.statementHtml: Read one ASCII word containing 1 to 20 letters, without spaces. Print Word: before input, then the reversed word. Use pair-swapping recursion.
hints: Find the length before calling reverse with length minus one.

practice.title: Print the Hanoi plan
practice.statementHtml: Read disk count from 0 to 5. Move from A to C using B. Print Disks: before input, then one SOURCE -> TARGET line per move; zero disks produces no move lines.
hints: Exchange peg roles separately for the two recursive calls.

practice.title: A recursive star triangle
practice.statementHtml: Read rows from 0 to 8. Print Rows: then rows of one through n stars, each ending with a newline. Use recursion for both rows and stars.
hints: Printing after the smaller triangle gives ascending row lengths.

quiz.prompt: Which argument shrinks in the shown simple power helper?
quiz.explanation: Each call subtracts one from a positive exponent until the zero-exponent case.

quiz.prompt: What is the chosen power-task result for base zero and exponent zero?
options: Undefined behavior in the integer helper
quiz.explanation: The task explicitly defines exponent zero as one, including this special input pair.

quiz.prompt: The recursive digit sum peels off 9, 0 and 4. Which sum is printed?
quiz.explanation: The contributions are nine, zero and four, totaling thirteen.

quiz.prompt: Which expression removes the last decimal digit of a nonnegative int?
quiz.explanation: Integer division removes the last digit; remainder obtains that last digit.

quiz.prompt: Why check b == 0 before Euclid remainder?
quiz.explanation: When b is zero the answer is already a, and no modulo operation should occur.

quiz.prompt: Euclid reduces the pair 48 and 18. Which divisor is returned?
quiz.explanation: The pairs become (18,12), (12,6) and (6,0), so the result is six.

quiz.prompt: What is the Hanoi move count for n disks?
quiz.explanation: Two smaller plans surround one largest-disk move, giving the stated recurrence.

quiz.prompt: Which range should a recursive binary search keep after its midpoint is too small?
quiz.explanation: The midpoint has already failed, so excluding it guarantees progress toward an empty interval.

quiz.prompt: A zero exponent ends immediately. Which pair of powers appears?
quiz.explanation: Three factors of negative two give negative eight; the empty product gives one.

quiz.prompt: Why use length minus one as the initial reversal right index?
options: The first letter is at index one
The final letter is at length plus one
The terminator at length must stay at the end
It forces every word to have even length
quiz.explanation: The length counts content characters; the trailing zero is not part of the reversed content.

quiz.prompt: Is byte-by-byte reversal a correct general Bangla UTF-8 reversal?
options: Yes, every character is one byte
Only when the buffer has static duration
No, multibyte encoding needs a different method
quiz.explanation: The practice deliberately uses ASCII words. UTF-8 characters may span several bytes.

quiz.prompt: What determines the leading cost of printing a recursive triangle with n rows?
options: The quadratic number of printed stars
Only the number of helper definitions
A constant number of printf calls
quiz.explanation: The total stars are n times n-plus-one divided by two, regardless of recursive organization.

quiz.prompt: Which peg role changes in the second recursive Hanoi move?
options: The target becomes the original source
The former spare becomes the source
The disk count becomes n plus one
quiz.explanation: After moving the largest disk, the smaller group begins on the old spare and moves to the target.

examQuestions.question: Derive the Hanoi move count and distinguish total calls from maximum active depth.
examQuestions.answerHtml: The zero-disk plan has no moves. The n-disk plan performs two n-minus-one plans and one largest-disk move, so T(n)=2T(n-1)+1=2^n-1. The branches run in sequence, giving linear maximum active depth despite exponential total work.

#include <stdio.h>

unsigned int digits(unsigned int n)
{
    if (n < 10) {
        return n;
    }
    return n % 10 + digits(n / 10);
}

int main(void)
{
    printf("%u\n", digits(409));
    return 0;
}

13

The contributions are nine, zero and four, totaling thirteen.

examQuestions.question: Read rows from 0 to 8. Print Rows: then rows of one through n stars, each ending with a newline. Use recursion for both rows and stars.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>

void stars(int n)
{
    if (n == 0) {
        return;
    }
    putchar('*');
    stars(n - 1);
}

void triangle(int rows)
{
    if (rows == 0) {
        return;
    }
    triangle(rows - 1);
    stars(rows);
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void)
{
    int rows;
    puts("Rows:");
    if (scanf("%d", &rows) != 1 || rows < 0 || rows > 8) {
        return 1;
    }
    triangle(rows);
    return 0;
}

Printing after the smaller triangle gives ascending row lengths.

For input 0, the program prints:

Rows:

examQuestions.question: Which peg role changes in the second recursive Hanoi move? Choose and justify: The target becomes the original source; The former spare becomes the source; All roles remain unchanged; The disk count becomes n plus one.
examQuestions.answerHtml: The former spare becomes the source. After moving the largest disk, the smaller group begins on the old spare and moves to the target.
